questions.prompt: Which keyword prevents a class from being inherited from?
questions.explanation: `sealed` stops further derivation (and can also be applied to an `override` to stop it being overridden again). `final` is the Java equivalent and isn't a C# keyword. `static` classes are implicitly sealed, but that's a side effect, not their purpose.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: `override` replaces the virtual method, so the runtime type (Dog) decides: "Dog speaks". `new` only *hides* the base method; it isn't polymorphic, so the compile-time type of the variable (Animal) decides: "Animal".

questions.prompt: Can a C# class inherit from more than one base class?
distractors: Only if all the base classes are abstract
Only if the class is marked partial
questions.explanation: C# has single inheritance for classes. A class can implement any number of interfaces, which is how you get multiple 'is-a' contracts without the diamond problem of multiple implementation inheritance.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an abstract class and an interface in modern C#?
questions.answer: An abstract class can hold instance state and constructors, but a class can inherit only one; an interface has no instance state, and a class can implement many.
distractors: Interfaces cannot contain any method bodies; abstract classes can.
Abstract classes cannot have constructors; interfaces can.
There is no difference since C# 8; they are interchangeable.
questions.explanation: Since C# 8, interfaces *can* have default method implementations (and static members), so 'no method bodies' is outdated. The lasting differences: abstract classes can have instance fields and constructors and use single inheritance; interfaces can't hold instance state, and a class can implement many of them.

questions.prompt: Can an interface declare instance fields in C#?
questions.explanation: Interfaces can never hold instance state. Since C# 8 they can have *static* fields and default method bodies, but per-object data needs a class (often an abstract base class). That is the most durable difference between the two.

questions.prompt: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
distractors: Only if it has no abstract members
questions.explanation: You can't `new` an abstract class directly, but derived classes call its constructor (via `: base(...)`) to initialise the shared state. Such constructors are usually `protected`. Interfaces can't have instance constructors at all.

questions.prompt: Since which C# version can interface members have a default implementation (a method body)?
questions.explanation: Default interface methods arrived in C# 8 (.NET Core 3.0) so library authors could add members to published interfaces without breaking implementers. C# 11 added *static abstract* interface members, which is a different feature.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: `Robot` doesn't implement `Greet`, so the interface's default body is used. `Person`'s public `Greet` implements the interface member (no `override` needed), so it wins. Note a default method is only reachable through the interface: `new Robot().Greet()` would not compile.

questions.prompt: Which C# 11 interface feature lets an interface require implementing types to provide a static method or operator (the basis of generic math)?
questions.explanation: `static abstract` members (e.g. `static abstract T operator +(T a, T b);`) let generic code call `T.Parse(...)` or `a + b` on a type parameter. This is how `INumber<T>` works. Default interface methods (C# 8) provide bodies for instance members instead.

questions.prompt: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?
questions.answer: When related types share state or implementation (fields, constructors, protected helpers) and form one 'is-a' family; an interface suits a capability unrelated types can share.
distractors: When a class needs to implement several of them at once.
When you want to define a contract with no implementation at all.
When you want structs to be able to implement it too.
questions.explanation: Abstract classes give shared code and state to a family of closely related types, at the cost of using up the single base class. Interfaces describe a capability (`IComparable`, `IDisposable`) that any class or struct can add, and a type can implement many.

questions.prompt: Which modifier declares a method with no body that every non-abstract derived class must override?
questions.explanation: An `abstract` method has no body and can only exist in an abstract class; concrete subclasses must override it. A `virtual` method has a body that derived classes *may* override. `partial` methods also have a separate declaration, but that's about splitting code across files, not inheritance.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an abstract method and a virtual method?
questions.answer: An abstract method has no body and must be overridden (and only exists in abstract classes); a virtual method has a default body that derived classes may override.
distractors: A virtual method has no body; an abstract method has a default body.
Abstract methods are resolved at compile time; virtual methods at run time.
Only virtual methods can be overridden with the override keyword.
questions.explanation: Both are overridden with `override` and both dispatch on the runtime type. The difference is whether there's a default: virtual = optional override with a fallback, abstract = mandatory override, no fallback.

questions.prompt: What is it called when a class has several methods with the same name but different parameter lists?
questions.explanation: Overloading = same name, different parameters, chosen by the compiler. Overriding = a derived class replacing a base class's virtual method with the same signature, chosen at run time.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Overload resolution happens at *compile time* using the variable's static type. `o` is declared as `object`, so `Print(object)` is chosen even though it holds a string. Only `virtual`/`override` dispatch looks at the runtime type.

questions.prompt: Which access modifier makes a type or member visible anywhere in the same assembly, but not outside it?
questions.explanation: `internal` = same assembly (project) only. `protected internal` is wider: same assembly *or* any derived class, even in another assembly.

questions.prompt: What is the default accessibility of a top-level class declared without an access modifier?
questions.explanation: Top-level types default to `internal`. Members inside a class default to `private`. The rule of thumb: C# defaults to the most restrictive access that makes sense, and a top-level type can't be private.

questions.prompt: What is the default accessibility of a field or method inside a class when no access modifier is written?
questions.explanation: Class (and struct) members default to `private`. Top-level types default to `internal`. Interface members default to `public`.

questions.prompt: Which access modifier means accessible from derived classes *or* from anywhere in the same assembly?
questions.explanation: `protected internal` is the union: protected OR internal. `private protected` (C# 7.2) is the intersection: derived classes AND same assembly. People often guess the opposite because the names read like an AND.

questions.prompt: Which access modifier means accessible only from derived classes that are *also* in the same assembly?
questions.explanation: `private protected` (C# 7.2) is protected AND internal: a subclass in another assembly can't see it. `protected internal` is the looser OR.

questions.prompt: Which OOP principle means hiding an object's internal state and only allowing changes through its own methods?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation protects invariants: fields are private and changes go through methods/properties that validate them. Abstraction is the related but different idea of exposing a simplified model of *what* something does.

questions.prompt: Which OOP principle lets code call the same method on objects of different types and get each type's own behaviour?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism ("many forms"): `shape.Area()` runs `Circle.Area` or `Square.Area` depending on the runtime type. Inheritance is one *mechanism* that enables it (interfaces are another), but it isn't the principle itself.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?
questions.answer: Abstraction decides what to expose (a simplified model or contract: the 'what'); encapsulation hides how it's done and protects internal state (the 'how').
distractors: They're the same principle with different names.
Abstraction means using abstract classes; encapsulation means using interfaces.
Encapsulation is about inheritance hierarchies; abstraction is about access modifiers.
questions.explanation: An `IPaymentGateway` with `Charge(amount)` is an abstraction: callers think in terms of charging, not HTTP. Making the API key and retry state private, reachable only through `Charge`, is encapsulation. They work together but answer different questions.

questions.prompt: Does composition model an 'is-a' or a 'has-a' relationship?
questions.explanation: Composition = an object *has* other objects as fields and delegates to them (a `Car` has an `Engine`). Inheritance = *is-a* (a `Car` is a `Vehicle`). 'Can-do' is how interfaces are often described. 'Favour composition over inheritance' because it's looser coupling.

questions.prompt: What is it called when a class implements an interface member so it can only be called through the interface type, e.g. `void IDisposable.Dispose()`?
questions.explanation: Explicit implementations have no access modifier and are hidden from the class's own public surface, so you must cast to the interface to call them. Uses: resolving two interfaces with the same member name, or keeping a rarely-used member out of IntelliSense.
